ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic released new visibility tools that let companies track exactly what they're getting for their AI spending before the company goes public. ai-at-work.title: Chrome’s AI-powered Autofill can now dig through your Gmail to fill out forms
ai-at-work.excerpt: The autofill update lets Chrome pull flight confirmations, tracking info, order details, and other information from your inbox, with your permission.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Chrome now lets its AI autofill feature scoop data from your Gmail inbox to populate forms faster, which sounds convenient until you think about it for five seconds. This matters because it's yet another integration point where your personal data lives in Google's ecosystem, and workplace tech teams need to understand what employees are consenting to when they use this. Look, I've been doing this thirty years and I've never seen a feature that made me think "finally, I want my browser reading my emails," so maybe we pump the brakes on the convenience train here.

tools-tech.dwp_take: Opera is rolling out locally-run AI models directly in its browser, letting enterprises process data on-device instead of shipping it to cloud providers. digital-culture.title: Thanks to AI, are we raising the first generation of kids who don’t have to figure things out?
digital-culture.excerpt: Your teenager gets into a fight with her best friend. She’s hurt, upset, and doesn’t know what to do. Maybe in the past she would have spent the day replaying the argument, venting to another friend a
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece asking whether AI is short-circuiting the problem-solving skills kids need to develop by handing them ready-made answers instead of forcing them to struggle through challenges. This matters to digital workplace leaders because today's teenagers are tomorrow's employees, and if they never learn to sit with discomfort or think through complex situations, your organization will eventually hire people who can't actually solve problems. The real workplace irony is that companies are frantically implementing AI to handle routine work while simultaneously raising a generation that won't know how to handle the non-routine stuff that actually requires a human brain.

digital-culture.title: There’s a career tax on being smart at work—but only if you’re a woman

digital-culture.dwp_take: Women who demonstrate competence and achievement at work often face social backlash and career penalties that men don't experience, according to research highlighted in this Fast Company piece about sales executive Sara Winslow. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because remote and hybrid work environments can actually amplify these dynamics through less visible social cues and harder-to-track exclusion patterns. Here's the brutal truth: we've spent three decades building better collaboration tools, but we haven't solved the ancient problem of people punishing women for being too good at their jobs, which means all your Slack channels and virtual whiteboarding software won't fix culture until you actually address it.
